PAGE 1: Learning outcomes

OVERVIEW
========

Mass tells how heavy an object is. In this sub-strand you will use a kilogramme, a half kilogramme and a quarter kilogramme with a beam balance, then add and subtract masses written in kilogrammes.

## Strand 2.0: Measurement
Sub-strand 2.5: Mass
Suggested lessons: 8

## What this sub-strand covers
• Mas in kilogrammes
• Addition and subtraction of mass

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Mathematics Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 Measurement, Sub-strand 2.5 Mass

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) use a kilogramme mass to measure masses of different objects practically
b) use 1⁄2 kg and 1⁄4 kg masses to measure masses of different objects practically
c) add mass involving kilogrammes in real- life situations
d) subtract mass involving kilogrammes in real- life situations
e) appreciate kilogramme as a unit of measuring mass

## Key inquiry questions
1. How can we measure mass in kilogrammes?

PAGE 2: How we will learn

## Learning experiences
• use one kilogramme (kg) masses to measure masses of given objects using a beam balance
• work with peers in making a 1⁄2 kg mass and use it to measure mass of given objects using a beam balance
• share tasks while making a 1⁄4 kg mass and use it to measure mass of given objects using a beam balance and an electronic balance
• add mass involving kilogrammes in real-life situations
• carry out subtraction of mass involving kilogrammes
• play digital games involving mass

## Core competencies
• Digital literacy: learner makes a 1⁄4 kg mass and uses it to measure mass of given objects using a beam balance and an electronic balance. Learner plays digital games involving mass.

## Values
• Integrity: learner displays humility in teams while making a 1⁄2 kg mass and accurately uses it to measure the mass of given objects using a beam balance.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Social Justice: learner shares resources equitably as they use beam balance.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate the measurement of the mass of given objects using a beam balance to properties of matter in Science and Technology.

PAGE 3: Lesson 1: The kilogramme and the beam balance

LESSON 1: THE KILOGRAMME AND THE BEAM BALANCE
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain that the kilogramme is a unit of mass.
• Say when a beam balance shows that two masses are equal.

Curriculum outcomes: a) use a kilogramme mass to measure masses of different objects practically; e) appreciate kilogramme as a unit of measuring mass

## Introduction
A packet of sugar and a packet of tea can be the same size and still not be equally heavy. Mass is the amount of matter in an object. We measure it in kilogrammes.

## Notes

The short way of writing kilogramme is kg. A 1 kg mass is a standard piece, often a metal weight marked 1 kg, used on a balance. Shops, markets and kitchens use the kilogramme so that a buyer receives the mass that was agreed.

### The beam balance
A beam balance has a bar that pivots in the middle and a pan on each side. Put the object in one pan. Put known kilogramme masses in the other pan.

- If the object's pan goes down, the object has more mass than the masses in the other pan.
- If the pan with the known masses goes down, those masses are heavier than the object.
- If the beam is level, the two sides have the same mass.

The balance must sit on a flat table. Hold the beam still, then let go gently. Do not press a pan down with your hand while you read it. That would make the two sides look equal when they are not.

PAGE 4: Lesson 1: The kilogramme and the beam balance — Example 1

### Mass is not size
A small stone can have more mass than a large empty box. You cannot judge the kilogrammes by looking. The balance gives the measurement.

An electronic balance shows the mass as a number on a screen. It must read zero before the object is placed on it. You will use both kinds of balance when you measure.

## Key words
• mass — the amount of matter in an object; how heavy it is
• kilogramme (kg) — the unit used to measure mass
• beam balance — a balance with a bar and two pans, used to compare masses

## Worked examples

### Example 1
An object is in one pan. Three masses of 1 kg are in the other pan, and the beam is level. What is the mass of the object?

Working:
1. A level beam means the two sides are equal.
2. 3 × 1 kg = 3 kg.

Answer: 3 kg

PAGE 5: Lesson 1: The kilogramme and the beam balance — Make the beam level

## Worked examples

### Example 2
The pan holding a bag goes down when 2 kg is on the other pan, but the beam is level when 3 kg is on the other pan. What is the mass of the bag?

Working:
1. The bag is heavier than 2 kg.
2. It balances 3 kg, so its mass is 3 kg.

Answer: 3 kg

## Activity: Make the beam level
You will need: Beam balance, 1 kg masses, A book, a stone and an empty tin

1. Set the beam balance on a flat desk and check that it hangs level when both pans are empty.

2. Place a book in one pan. Add 1 kg masses to the other pan until the beam is level, or until you can say the mass is between two whole kilogrammes.

3. Repeat with a stone and with an empty tin.

4. Each group member should have a turn to add or remove a mass. Share the balance fairly.

5. Return the masses to their box so that they are not dropped or lost.

PAGE 6: Lesson 2: Measuring mass with one-kilogramme masses

## Practice

1. What does a level beam tell you about the two pans?

2. Four masses of 1 kg balance a bag of maize flour. What is the mass of the bag?

3. Why can a small stone have more mass than a large empty box?

## Answers to practice

1. The masses on the two sides are equal.

2. 4 kg

3. Mass is not the same as size. The balance, not the look of the object, tells the mass.

## Summary
• The kilogramme (kg) is the unit of mass.
• On a beam balance, a level beam means the two masses are equal.
• Do not press the pan while you read the balance.

LESSON 2: MEASURING MASS WITH ONE-KILOGRAMME MASSES
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Measure the mass of an object using 1 kg masses.
• Record a mass that falls between two whole kilogrammes.

Curriculum outcomes: a) use a kilogramme mass to measure masses of different objects practically

## Introduction
A shopkeeper puts iron masses on one side of a balance and maize flour on the other. Counting the iron masses tells the mass of the flour.

## Notes

Use only masses that are marked 1 kg. Count them when the beam is level.

If 5 masses of 1 kg balance a sack, the sack has a mass of 5 kg. Write the unit. The number 5 could mean 5 grams or 5 items if you leave the unit out. In this lesson the unit is the kilogramme.

PAGE 7: Lesson 2: Measuring mass with one-kilogramme masses — Between two kilogrammes

### Between two kilogrammes
Sometimes no whole number of 1 kg masses makes the beam level.

- With 2 kg in the pan, the object side goes down, so the object is more than 2 kg.
- With 3 kg in the pan, the mass side goes down, so the object is less than 3 kg.

The mass is between 2 kg and 3 kg. You need a smaller mass, such as ½ kg, to measure it more closely. Do not call it 2 kg or 3 kg if the beam is not level.

### Adding two objects
If a 2 kg packet and a 3 kg packet are placed together in one pan, they balance 5 masses of 1 kg. The total mass is 2 + 3 = 5 kg. Measuring them together checks the addition.

Handle the metal masses with dry hands. Do not drop them onto the pan. A bent pan or a chipped mass will not measure fairly. When several groups share one balance, take turns and leave it level for the next group.

## Key words
• standard mass — a marked piece, such as a 1 kg mass, used to measure other objects
• between — more than one whole kilogramme and less than the next

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Five masses of 1 kg balance a bag of flour. What is the mass of the bag?

Working:
1. Each mass is 1 kg.
2. 5 × 1 kg = 5 kg, and the beam is level.

Answer: 5 kg

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A 2 kg packet and a 3 kg packet are put in the same pan. How many 1 kg masses balance them?

Working:
1. 2 + 3 = 5.
2. Five masses of 1 kg are needed.

Answer: 5 masses, because the total is 5 kg

PAGE 8: Lesson 2: Measuring mass with one-kilogramme masses — Practice

## Activity: Count the kilogrammes
You will need: Beam balance, Several 1 kg masses, Classroom objects such as a bag of books

1. Choose an object and estimate whether it is less than 1 kg, about 1 kg, or more than 1 kg.

2. Measure it with 1 kg masses. Record the mass if the beam is level.

3. If the beam is not level, write the two whole kilogrammes it lies between.

4. Put two measured objects in one pan and check that their total matches the sum you calculated.

5. Share the masses so that every learner handles the balance once.

## Practice

1. Six masses of 1 kg balance a bunch of bananas. What is the mass of the bananas?

2. An object is heavier than 4 kg but lighter than 5 kg, and the beam is not level with either. What can you say about its mass?

3. A 4 kg tin and a 1 kg stone are weighed together. What total mass should balance them?

## Answers to practice

1. 6 kg

2. Its mass is between 4 kg and 5 kg.

3. 5 kg

## Summary
• Count the 1 kg masses when the beam is level.
• If the beam will not level, the mass lies between two whole kilogrammes.
• Write kg in the answer.

PAGE 9: Lesson 3: Half-kilogramme and quarter-kilogramme masses

LESSON 3: HALF-KILOGRAMME AND QUARTER-KILOGRAMME MASSES
=======================================================

## What you will learn
• Show that 2 half kilogrammes make 1 kg and 4 quarter kilogrammes make 1 kg.
• Measure an object using ½ kg and ¼ kg masses.

Curriculum outcomes: b) use 1⁄2 kg and 1⁄4 kg masses to measure masses of different objects practically

## Introduction
A small packet of sugar may be only half a kilogramme. A beam balance can check that half, and an electronic balance can show the same mass as a number.

## Notes

Half a kilogramme is written ½ kg. A quarter of a kilogramme is written ¼ kg.

2 × ½ kg = 1 kg

4 × ¼ kg = 1 kg

2 × ¼ kg = ½ kg

PAGE 10: Lesson 3: Half-kilogramme and quarter-kilogramme masses — Measuring

### Making a half kilogramme
Put a 1 kg mass in one pan. In the other pan, put two light tins. Add dry sand or beans a little at a time until the beam is level. Then balance the two tins against each other. Move sand until those two tins match. Each tin is now ½ kg, and the two tins together still balance the 1 kg mass.

### Making a quarter kilogramme
Split one ½ kg tin into two equal tins in the same way. Each new tin is ¼ kg. Four of them should balance the original 1 kg mass.

### Measuring
An object that balances three ½ kg masses has mass 3 × ½ kg = 1½ kg.

An object that balances five ¼ kg masses has mass 5 × ¼ kg = 1¼ kg.

On an electronic balance, set the reading to zero, place the object gently, and read the screen. A reading of 1.5 kg is the same as 1½ kg. A reading of 0.25 kg is the same as ¼ kg. If you do not yet read decimals easily, match the object with ½ kg and ¼ kg masses on the beam balance as well.

Work calmly so that sand is not spilled into the pans. Wipe the desk and return every mass.

PAGE 11: Lesson 3: Half-kilogramme and quarter-kilogramme masses — Example 1

## Key words
• half kilogramme — ½ kg, one of two equal parts of a kilogramme
• quarter kilogramme — ¼ kg, one of four equal parts of a kilogramme

## Worked examples

### Example 1
An object balances three masses of ½ kg. What is its mass?

Working:
1. 3 × ½ kg = 3/2 kg.
2. 3/2 kg = 1½ kg.

Answer: 1½ kg

## Worked examples

### Example 2
How many quarter-kilogramme masses make 2 kg?

Working:
1. 1 kg = 4 quarter kilogrammes.
2. 2 × 4 = 8.

Answer: 8 quarter-kilogramme masses

## Worked examples

### Example 3
Five masses of ¼ kg balance a packet. What is the mass of the packet?

Working:
1. 5 × ¼ kg = 5/4 kg = 1¼ kg.

Answer: 1¼ kg

PAGE 12: Lesson 3: Half-kilogramme and quarter-kilogramme masses — Make a half and a quarter

## Activity: Make a half and a quarter
You will need: Beam balance, A 1 kg mass, Dry sand or beans, Small tins or bags, An electronic balance if the school has one

1. With a partner, make two equal ½ kg masses that together balance 1 kg.

2. Use one of them to make two ¼ kg masses. Check that four quarter masses balance 1 kg.

3. Measure a small classroom object with your ½ kg and ¼ kg masses.

4. If an electronic balance is available, set it to zero and measure the same object. Compare the reading with your beam-balance result.

5. Pour the sand back into its container. Do not leave it on the floor.

## Practice

1. How many half kilogrammes make 4 kg?

2. How many quarter kilogrammes make 1 half kilogramme?

3. An object balances one 1 kg mass and one ½ kg mass. What is its mass?

4. An electronic balance reads 0.25 kg. What fraction of a kilogramme is that?

## Answers to practice

1. 8 half kilogrammes

2. 2 quarter kilogrammes

3. 1½ kg

4. ¼ kg

## Summary
• 2 × ½ kg = 1 kg and 4 × ¼ kg = 1 kg.
• Make smaller masses by splitting a known mass into parts that balance each other.
• 1½ kg is the same as 1.5 kg on an electronic balance.

PAGE 13: Lesson 4: Adding mass in kilogrammes

LESSON 4: ADDING MASS IN KILOGRAMMES
====================================

## What you will learn
• Add whole-kilogramme masses, regrouping where a column is 10 or more.
• Add masses that include halves and quarters of a kilogramme.

Curriculum outcomes: c) add mass involving kilogrammes in real- life situations

## Introduction
A farmer sends 48 kg of potatoes in one sack and 37 kg in another. The total mass is what the buyer pays for. You find it by adding kilogrammes.

## Notes

Add the numbers in columns, ones first. Carry when a column comes to 10 or more. Write kg in the total.

### Whole kilogrammes
Add 48 kg and 37 kg.

- Ones: 8 + 7 = 15. Write 5, carry 1 ten.
- Tens: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8.
- The total is 85 kg.

Add 156 kg and 89 kg.

- Ones: 6 + 9 = 15. Write 5, carry 1.
- Tens: 5 + 8 + 1 = 14. Write 4, carry 1 hundred.
- Hundreds: 1 + 1 = 2.
- The total is 245 kg.

Check by adding in the other order.

PAGE 14: Lesson 4: Adding mass in kilogrammes — Example 2

### Halves and quarters
Add the fraction parts, then the whole kilogrammes. Change 2 quarters into a half, and 2 halves into a kilogramme.

2½ kg + 1¾ kg:

- Wholes: 2 + 1 = 3.
- Fractions: ½ + ¾ = 1¼, because 2 quarters + 3 quarters = 5 quarters = 1¼.
- 3 + 1¼ = 4¼ kg.

1½ kg + ½ kg = 2 kg, because the two halves make another kilogramme.

You can check a small total on the beam balance by putting both objects in one pan. The known masses that balance them should match your addition.

## Key words
• total mass — the mass when two or more masses are added
• carry — to move 10 from one column into 1 in the next column

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Add 48 kg and 37 kg.

Working:
1. Ones: 8 + 7 = 15. Write 5, carry 1.
2. Tens: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8.

Answer: 85 kg

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Add 156 kg and 89 kg.

Working:
1. Ones: 6 + 9 = 15. Write 5, carry 1.
2. Tens: 5 + 8 + 1 = 14. Write 4, carry 1.
3. Hundreds: 1 + 1 = 2.

Answer: 245 kg

## Worked examples

### Example 3
Add 2½ kg and 1¾ kg.

Working:
1. ½ + ¾ = 1¼.
2. 2 + 1 + 1¼ = 4¼.

Answer: 4¼ kg

PAGE 15: Lesson 4: Adding mass in kilogrammes — Practice

## Activity: Add two masses
You will need: Beam balance, 1 kg, ½ kg and ¼ kg masses, Two small bags of sand, Exercise book

1. Measure the mass of each bag using kilogramme masses.

2. Add the two masses in your book.

3. Put both bags in one pan and measure the total. Compare it with your addition.

4. Work out 156 kg + 89 kg in columns, then add 89 kg + 156 kg as a check.

5. Take turns recording the answer so that one person does not do all the writing.

## Practice

1. Add 64 kg and 29 kg.

2. Add 275 kg and 148 kg.

3. Add 1½ kg and ¾ kg.

4. A trader has 1,250 kg of maize and buys 875 kg more. What is the total mass?

## Answers to practice

1. 93 kg

2. 423 kg

3. 2¼ kg

4. 2,125 kg

## Summary
• Add kilogrammes in columns and carry when a column is 10 or more.
• Add halves and quarters, changing 2 halves into 1 kg.
• Check by adding in the other order, or by weighing both objects together.

PAGE 16: Lesson 5: Subtracting mass in kilogrammes

LESSON 5: SUBTRACTING MASS IN KILOGRAMMES
=========================================

## What you will learn
• Subtract kilogrammes, regrouping when a digit is too small.
• Subtract halves and quarters of a kilogramme.

Curriculum outcomes: d) subtract mass involving kilogrammes in real- life situations

## Introduction
A store had 70 kg of beans. Customers bought 28 kg. Subtraction tells you the mass that is still in the store. You can check a small subtraction on the beam balance.

## Notes

Write the larger mass on top. Subtract the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds. If a top digit is smaller than the digit below it, regroup.

### Whole kilogrammes
Subtract 28 kg from 70 kg.

- Ones: 0 is smaller than 8. Regroup 1 ten. The tens become 6, and the ones become 10.
- 10 − 8 = 2.
- Tens: 6 − 2 = 4.
- 42 kg remain.

Subtract 175 kg from 400 kg.

- Ones: regroup, 10 − 5 = 5.
- Tens: the tens digit became 9 after regrouping from the hundreds, then 9 − 7 = 2.
- Hundreds: 3 − 1 = 2.
- 225 kg remain.

Check: 225 + 175 = 400.

PAGE 17: Lesson 5: Subtracting mass in kilogrammes — Key words

### Halves and quarters
5 kg − 1½ kg. First take away 1 kg, leaving 4 kg. Then take away ½ kg, leaving 3½ kg.

1 kg − ¼ kg = ¾ kg.

½ kg − ¼ kg = ¼ kg.

2¼ kg − ¾ kg: the quarters are 1 quarter minus 3 quarters, so regroup 1 whole as 4 quarters. You then have 1 whole and 5 quarters, minus 3 quarters, which is 1 whole and 2 quarters. Two quarters are a half, so the answer is 1½ kg.

On a balance, you can check 1 kg − ¼ kg by removing a ¼ kg mass from a 1 kg side and seeing that ¾ kg remains to balance it.

## Key words
• difference in mass — how much heavier one object is, or how much mass is left
• regroup — to change 1 ten into 10 ones, or 1 kg into halves or quarters, so you can subtract

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Subtract 28 kg from 70 kg.

Working:
1. Regroup 1 ten: 10 − 8 = 2.
2. Tens: 6 − 2 = 4.

Answer: 42 kg

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Subtract 175 kg from 400 kg.

Working:
1. 400 − 175.
2. Check by adding 225 + 175.

Answer: 225 kg

## Worked examples

### Example 3
Subtract 1½ kg from 5 kg.

Working:
1. 5 − 1 = 4.
2. 4 − ½ = 3½.

Answer: 3½ kg

PAGE 18: Lesson 5: Subtracting mass in kilogrammes — Mass left on the pan

## Activity: Mass left on the pan
You will need: Beam balance, 1 kg and ¼ kg masses, A bag of sand, Exercise book

1. Make a bag of sand with mass 1 kg. Remove sand until the bag balances ¾ kg. Say which subtraction you did.

2. In your book, subtract 28 kg from 70 kg and check by adding.

3. Solve 2¼ kg − ¾ kg and explain the regrouping of 1 kg into quarters.

4. Write one real situation, such as selling maize or using cooking fat, where you subtract mass.

5. If you can, play a digital game about mass and record one subtraction from it.

## Practice

1. Subtract 46 kg from 90 kg.

2. A store had 500 kg of rice and sold 275 kg. How much rice is left?

3. Subtract ¾ kg from 2¼ kg.

4. How do you check that 400 − 175 = 225?

## Answers to practice

1. 44 kg

2. 225 kg

3. 1½ kg

4. Add 225 and 175. The sum should be 400.

## Summary
• Subtract kilogrammes in columns, regrouping when you need to.
• Check by adding the answer to the mass that was taken away.
• Change 1 kg into quarters when the fraction on top is too small.

PAGE 19: Lesson 6: Using the kilogramme in daily life — A fair measurement

LESSON 6: USING THE KILOGRAMME IN DAILY LIFE
============================================

## What you will learn
• Describe work in which people measure mass in kilogrammes.
• Explain why an accurate mass is fair to both the buyer and the seller.

Curriculum outcomes: e) appreciate kilogramme as a unit of measuring mass

## Introduction
Bread, sugar, maize flour, meat and animal feed are sold by the kilogramme. A correct balance protects the customer and the seller.

## Notes

People use the kilogramme in many jobs.

- A shopkeeper weighs flour, rice, sugar and beans.
- A farmer weighs a harvest before taking it to market.
- A cook measures ingredients so that a recipe turns out as planned.
- A health worker may record a person's mass as one fact about growth. That reading is done on a proper scale, not guessed.
- A builder orders sand or cement by the kilogramme or by a known bag size.

### A fair measurement
If a beam is not level and the seller still calls the mass 2 kg, the customer may receive less than 2 kg. If the masses themselves are wrong, both sides are cheated. Using a true 1 kg, ½ kg or ¼ kg mass, and waiting until the beam is level, is an honest measurement.

An electronic balance must start at zero. A container left on the balance adds its own mass. Put the container on first, set the reading back to zero, then add the food. The screen then shows the mass of the food only.

### Sharing the tools
In class, one balance serves many learners. Each person needs a turn to measure, and the masses must be put back so the next group can work. That is a fair use of a shared tool.

The kilogramme is worth learning because it is the same unit in a market, a shop and a store. Once you can add and subtract kilogrammes, you can find a total order or the mass that remains after a sale.

PAGE 20: Lesson 6: Using the kilogramme in daily life — A fair market stall

## Key words
• accurate — measured carefully so that the result matches the true mass
• zero — the reading on an electronic balance before the object is placed, or after a container is set aside

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A customer buys 2 kg of beans and 1½ kg of rice. What is the total mass?

Working:
1. 2 + 1½ = 3½.
2. The shopkeeper should pack 3½ kg altogether.

Answer: 3½ kg

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A sack of 50 kg has 12 kg sold from it. What mass remains?

Working:
1. 50 − 12 = 38.

Answer: 38 kg

## Activity: A fair market stall
You will need: Beam balance, 1 kg and ½ kg masses, Bags of sand to stand for food, Price cards are not needed

1. Role-play a seller and a buyer. The buyer asks for 1½ kg of 'beans' made from sand.

2. The seller measures 1 kg and ½ kg while the buyer watches the beam.

3. The buyer checks that the beam is level before accepting the bag.

4. Swap roles. Then subtract: if 2 kg was on the table and 1½ kg was sold, what mass is left?

5. Talk about why both people should be able to see the balance.

PAGE 21: Revision quiz

## Practice

1. A cook uses 1½ kg of flour and ½ kg of sugar. What is the total mass of the two ingredients?

2. A farmer harvested 86 kg of beans and kept 29 kg for the family. What mass can be taken to market?

3. Why should an electronic balance read zero before you put food on it?

4. Name two workers who measure mass in kilogrammes.

## Answers to practice

1. 2 kg

2. 57 kg

3. So that the screen shows the mass of the food, and not an old reading or the mass of an empty container.

4. Any two, such as a shopkeeper, a farmer, a cook or a health worker.

## Summary
• The kilogramme is used for food, farm produce and many goods.
• A level beam, true masses and a zeroed electronic balance give a fair measure.
• Add to find a total order and subtract to find what remains.

REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. When is the mass of an object equal to the masses in the other pan of a beam balance?
   A. When the object pan is down
   B. When the beam is level
   C. When the mass pan is down

2. Five masses of 1 kg balance a bag. What is the mass of the bag?

3. How many half kilogrammes make 3 kg?
   A. 3
   B. 5
   C. 6
   D. 8

4. An object balances three masses of ½ kg. What is its mass?

5. How many quarter kilogrammes make 2 kg?

6. Add 48 kg and 37 kg.
   A. 75 kg
   B. 85 kg
   C. 85 g
   D. 11 kg

7. Add 2½ kg and 1¾ kg.

8. Subtract 28 kg from 70 kg.

9. Subtract 175 kg from 400 kg.
   A. 225 kg
   B. 235 kg
   C. 375 kg
   D. 575 kg

10. Why should a seller wait until the beam is level before saying the mass is 2 kg?

PAGE 22: Quiz answers

ANSWERS
=======

1. B. When the beam is level
   A level beam means the two sides have the same mass.

2. 5 kg
   5 × 1 kg = 5 kg.

3. C. 6
   Each kilogramme has 2 halves, so 3 × 2 = 6.

4. 1½ kg
   3 × ½ = 1½ kg.

5. 8
   Each kilogramme has 4 quarters, so 2 × 4 = 8.

6. B. 85 kg
   8 + 7 = 15, write 5 carry 1; 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. The total is 85 kg.

7. 4¼ kg
   ½ + ¾ = 1¼, and 2 + 1 + 1¼ = 4¼ kg.

8. 42 kg
   70 − 28 = 42.

9. A. 225 kg
   400 − 175 = 225. Check: 225 + 175 = 400.

10. Only a level beam shows that the goods really have a mass of 2 kg.
   If the beam is not level, the customer may get more or less than 2 kg.

studyPages.title: Learning outcomes
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Mass tells how heavy an object is. In this sub-strand you will use a kilogramme, a half kilogramme and a quarter kilogramme with a beam balance, then add and subtract masses written in kilogrammes.

## Strand 2.0: Measurement
Sub-strand 2.5: Mass
Suggested lessons: 8

## What this sub-strand covers
• Mas in kilogrammes
• Addition and subtraction of mass

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Mathematics Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 Measurement, Sub-strand 2.5 Mass

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) use a kilogramme mass to measure masses of different objects practically
b) use 1⁄2 kg and 1⁄4 kg masses to measure masses of different objects practically
c) add mass involving kilogrammes in real- life situations
d) subtract mass involving kilogrammes in real- life situations
e) appreciate kilogramme as a unit of measuring mass

## Key inquiry questions
1. How can we measure mass in kilogrammes?

studyPages.title: How we will learn
studyPages.body:
## Learning experiences
• use one kilogramme (kg) masses to measure masses of given objects using a beam balance
• work with peers in making a 1⁄2 kg mass and use it to measure mass of given objects using a beam balance
• share tasks while making a 1⁄4 kg mass and use it to measure mass of given objects using a beam balance and an electronic balance
• add mass involving kilogrammes in real-life situations
• carry out subtraction of mass involving kilogrammes
• play digital games involving mass

## Core competencies
• Digital literacy: learner makes a 1⁄4 kg mass and uses it to measure mass of given objects using a beam balance and an electronic balance. Learner plays digital games involving mass.

## Values
• Integrity: learner displays humility in teams while making a 1⁄2 kg mass and accurately uses it to measure the mass of given objects using a beam balance.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Social Justice: learner shares resources equitably as they use beam balance.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate the measurement of the mass of given objects using a beam balance to properties of matter in Science and Technology.

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: The kilogramme and the beam balance
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: THE KILOGRAMME AND THE BEAM BALANCE
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain that the kilogramme is a unit of mass.
• Say when a beam balance shows that two masses are equal.

Curriculum outcomes: a) use a kilogramme mass to measure masses of different objects practically; e) appreciate kilogramme as a unit of measuring mass

## Introduction
A packet of sugar and a packet of tea can be the same size and still not be equally heavy. Mass is the amount of matter in an object. We measure it in kilogrammes.

## Notes

The short way of writing kilogramme is kg. A 1 kg mass is a standard piece, often a metal weight marked 1 kg, used on a balance. Shops, markets and kitchens use the kilogramme so that a buyer receives the mass that was agreed.

### The beam balance
A beam balance has a bar that pivots in the middle and a pan on each side. Put the object in one pan. Put known kilogramme masses in the other pan.

- If the object's pan goes down, the object has more mass than the masses in the other pan.
- If the pan with the known masses goes down, those masses are heavier than the object.
- If the beam is level, the two sides have the same mass.

The balance must sit on a flat table. Hold the beam still, then let go gently. Do not press a pan down with your hand while you read it. That would make the two sides look equal when they are not.

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: The kilogramme and the beam balance — Example 1
studyPages.body:
### Mass is not size
A small stone can have more mass than a large empty box. You cannot judge the kilogrammes by looking. The balance gives the measurement.

An electronic balance shows the mass as a number on a screen. It must read zero before the object is placed on it. You will use both kinds of balance when you measure.

## Key words
• mass — the amount of matter in an object; how heavy it is
• kilogramme (kg) — the unit used to measure mass
• beam balance — a balance with a bar and two pans, used to compare masses

## Worked examples

### Example 1
An object is in one pan. Three masses of 1 kg are in the other pan, and the beam is level. What is the mass of the object?

Working:
1. A level beam means the two sides are equal.
2. 3 × 1 kg = 3 kg.

Answer: 3 kg

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: The kilogramme and the beam balance — Make the beam level
studyPages.body:
## Worked examples

### Example 2
The pan holding a bag goes down when 2 kg is on the other pan, but the beam is level when 3 kg is on the other pan. What is the mass of the bag?

Working:
1. The bag is heavier than 2 kg.
2. It balances 3 kg, so its mass is 3 kg.

Answer: 3 kg

## Activity: Make the beam level
You will need: Beam balance, 1 kg masses, A book, a stone and an empty tin

1. Set the beam balance on a flat desk and check that it hangs level when both pans are empty.

2. Place a book in one pan. Add 1 kg masses to the other pan until the beam is level, or until you can say the mass is between two whole kilogrammes.

3. Repeat with a stone and with an empty tin.

4. Each group member should have a turn to add or remove a mass. Share the balance fairly.

5. Return the masses to their box so that they are not dropped or lost.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Measuring mass with one-kilogramme masses
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. What does a level beam tell you about the two pans?

2. Four masses of 1 kg balance a bag of maize flour. What is the mass of the bag?

3. Why can a small stone have more mass than a large empty box?

## Answers to practice

1. The masses on the two sides are equal.

2. 4 kg

3. Mass is not the same as size. The balance, not the look of the object, tells the mass.

## Summary
• The kilogramme (kg) is the unit of mass.
• On a beam balance, a level beam means the two masses are equal.
• Do not press the pan while you read the balance.

LESSON 2: MEASURING MASS WITH ONE-KILOGRAMME MASSES
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Measure the mass of an object using 1 kg masses.
• Record a mass that falls between two whole kilogrammes.

Curriculum outcomes: a) use a kilogramme mass to measure masses of different objects practically

## Introduction
A shopkeeper puts iron masses on one side of a balance and maize flour on the other. Counting the iron masses tells the mass of the flour.

## Notes

Use only masses that are marked 1 kg. Count them when the beam is level.

If 5 masses of 1 kg balance a sack, the sack has a mass of 5 kg. Write the unit. The number 5 could mean 5 grams or 5 items if you leave the unit out. In this lesson the unit is the kilogramme.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Measuring mass with one-kilogramme masses — Between two kilogrammes
studyPages.body:
### Between two kilogrammes
Sometimes no whole number of 1 kg masses makes the beam level.

- With 2 kg in the pan, the object side goes down, so the object is more than 2 kg.
- With 3 kg in the pan, the mass side goes down, so the object is less than 3 kg.

The mass is between 2 kg and 3 kg. You need a smaller mass, such as ½ kg, to measure it more closely. Do not call it 2 kg or 3 kg if the beam is not level.

### Adding two objects
If a 2 kg packet and a 3 kg packet are placed together in one pan, they balance 5 masses of 1 kg. The total mass is 2 + 3 = 5 kg. Measuring them together checks the addition.

Handle the metal masses with dry hands. Do not drop them onto the pan. A bent pan or a chipped mass will not measure fairly. When several groups share one balance, take turns and leave it level for the next group.

## Key words
• standard mass — a marked piece, such as a 1 kg mass, used to measure other objects
• between — more than one whole kilogramme and less than the next

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Five masses of 1 kg balance a bag of flour. What is the mass of the bag?

Working:
1. Each mass is 1 kg.
2. 5 × 1 kg = 5 kg, and the beam is level.

Answer: 5 kg

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A 2 kg packet and a 3 kg packet are put in the same pan. How many 1 kg masses balance them?

Working:
1. 2 + 3 = 5.
2. Five masses of 1 kg are needed.

Answer: 5 masses, because the total is 5 kg

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Measuring mass with one-kilogramme masses — Practice
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Count the kilogrammes
You will need: Beam balance, Several 1 kg masses, Classroom objects such as a bag of books

1. Choose an object and estimate whether it is less than 1 kg, about 1 kg, or more than 1 kg.

2. Measure it with 1 kg masses. Record the mass if the beam is level.

3. If the beam is not level, write the two whole kilogrammes it lies between.

4. Put two measured objects in one pan and check that their total matches the sum you calculated.

5. Share the masses so that every learner handles the balance once.

## Practice

1. Six masses of 1 kg balance a bunch of bananas. What is the mass of the bananas?

2. An object is heavier than 4 kg but lighter than 5 kg, and the beam is not level with either. What can you say about its mass?

3. A 4 kg tin and a 1 kg stone are weighed together. What total mass should balance them?

## Answers to practice

1. 6 kg

2. Its mass is between 4 kg and 5 kg.

3. 5 kg

## Summary
• Count the 1 kg masses when the beam is level.
• If the beam will not level, the mass lies between two whole kilogrammes.
• Write kg in the answer.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Half-kilogramme and quarter-kilogramme masses
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: HALF-KILOGRAMME AND QUARTER-KILOGRAMME MASSES
=======================================================

## What you will learn
• Show that 2 half kilogrammes make 1 kg and 4 quarter kilogrammes make 1 kg.
• Measure an object using ½ kg and ¼ kg masses.

Curriculum outcomes: b) use 1⁄2 kg and 1⁄4 kg masses to measure masses of different objects practically

## Introduction
A small packet of sugar may be only half a kilogramme. A beam balance can check that half, and an electronic balance can show the same mass as a number.

## Notes

Half a kilogramme is written ½ kg. A quarter of a kilogramme is written ¼ kg.

2 × ½ kg = 1 kg

4 × ¼ kg = 1 kg

2 × ¼ kg = ½ kg

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Half-kilogramme and quarter-kilogramme masses — Measuring
studyPages.body:
### Making a half kilogramme
Put a 1 kg mass in one pan. In the other pan, put two light tins. Add dry sand or beans a little at a time until the beam is level. Then balance the two tins against each other. Move sand until those two tins match. Each tin is now ½ kg, and the two tins together still balance the 1 kg mass.

### Making a quarter kilogramme
Split one ½ kg tin into two equal tins in the same way. Each new tin is ¼ kg. Four of them should balance the original 1 kg mass.

### Measuring
An object that balances three ½ kg masses has mass 3 × ½ kg = 1½ kg.

An object that balances five ¼ kg masses has mass 5 × ¼ kg = 1¼ kg.

On an electronic balance, set the reading to zero, place the object gently, and read the screen. A reading of 1.5 kg is the same as 1½ kg. A reading of 0.25 kg is the same as ¼ kg. If you do not yet read decimals easily, match the object with ½ kg and ¼ kg masses on the beam balance as well.

Work calmly so that sand is not spilled into the pans. Wipe the desk and return every mass.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Half-kilogramme and quarter-kilogramme masses — Example 1
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• half kilogramme — ½ kg, one of two equal parts of a kilogramme
• quarter kilogramme — ¼ kg, one of four equal parts of a kilogramme

## Worked examples

### Example 1
An object balances three masses of ½ kg. What is its mass?

Working:
1. 3 × ½ kg = 3/2 kg.
2. 3/2 kg = 1½ kg.

Answer: 1½ kg

## Worked examples

### Example 2
How many quarter-kilogramme masses make 2 kg?

Working:
1. 1 kg = 4 quarter kilogrammes.
2. 2 × 4 = 8.

Answer: 8 quarter-kilogramme masses

## Worked examples

### Example 3
Five masses of ¼ kg balance a packet. What is the mass of the packet?

Working:
1. 5 × ¼ kg = 5/4 kg = 1¼ kg.

Answer: 1¼ kg

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Half-kilogramme and quarter-kilogramme masses — Make a half and a quarter
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Make a half and a quarter
You will need: Beam balance, A 1 kg mass, Dry sand or beans, Small tins or bags, An electronic balance if the school has one

1. With a partner, make two equal ½ kg masses that together balance 1 kg.

2. Use one of them to make two ¼ kg masses. Check that four quarter masses balance 1 kg.

3. Measure a small classroom object with your ½ kg and ¼ kg masses.

4. If an electronic balance is available, set it to zero and measure the same object. Compare the reading with your beam-balance result.

5. Pour the sand back into its container. Do not leave it on the floor.

## Practice

1. How many half kilogrammes make 4 kg?

2. How many quarter kilogrammes make 1 half kilogramme?

3. An object balances one 1 kg mass and one ½ kg mass. What is its mass?

4. An electronic balance reads 0.25 kg. What fraction of a kilogramme is that?

## Answers to practice

1. 8 half kilogrammes

2. 2 quarter kilogrammes

3. 1½ kg

4. ¼ kg

## Summary
• 2 × ½ kg = 1 kg and 4 × ¼ kg = 1 kg.
• Make smaller masses by splitting a known mass into parts that balance each other.
• 1½ kg is the same as 1.5 kg on an electronic balance.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Adding mass in kilogrammes
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: ADDING MASS IN KILOGRAMMES
====================================

## What you will learn
• Add whole-kilogramme masses, regrouping where a column is 10 or more.
• Add masses that include halves and quarters of a kilogramme.

Curriculum outcomes: c) add mass involving kilogrammes in real- life situations

## Introduction
A farmer sends 48 kg of potatoes in one sack and 37 kg in another. The total mass is what the buyer pays for. You find it by adding kilogrammes.

## Notes

Add the numbers in columns, ones first. Carry when a column comes to 10 or more. Write kg in the total.

### Whole kilogrammes
Add 48 kg and 37 kg.

- Ones: 8 + 7 = 15. Write 5, carry 1 ten.
- Tens: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8.
- The total is 85 kg.

Add 156 kg and 89 kg.

- Ones: 6 + 9 = 15. Write 5, carry 1.
- Tens: 5 + 8 + 1 = 14. Write 4, carry 1 hundred.
- Hundreds: 1 + 1 = 2.
- The total is 245 kg.

Check by adding in the other order.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Adding mass in kilogrammes — Example 2
studyPages.body:
### Halves and quarters
Add the fraction parts, then the whole kilogrammes. Change 2 quarters into a half, and 2 halves into a kilogramme.

2½ kg + 1¾ kg:

- Wholes: 2 + 1 = 3.
- Fractions: ½ + ¾ = 1¼, because 2 quarters + 3 quarters = 5 quarters = 1¼.
- 3 + 1¼ = 4¼ kg.

1½ kg + ½ kg = 2 kg, because the two halves make another kilogramme.

You can check a small total on the beam balance by putting both objects in one pan. The known masses that balance them should match your addition.

## Key words
• total mass — the mass when two or more masses are added
• carry — to move 10 from one column into 1 in the next column

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Add 48 kg and 37 kg.

Working:
1. Ones: 8 + 7 = 15. Write 5, carry 1.
2. Tens: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8.

Answer: 85 kg

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Add 156 kg and 89 kg.

Working:
1. Ones: 6 + 9 = 15. Write 5, carry 1.
2. Tens: 5 + 8 + 1 = 14. Write 4, carry 1.
3. Hundreds: 1 + 1 = 2.

Answer: 245 kg

## Worked examples

### Example 3
Add 2½ kg and 1¾ kg.

Working:
1. ½ + ¾ = 1¼.
2. 2 + 1 + 1¼ = 4¼.

Answer: 4¼ kg

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Adding mass in kilogrammes — Practice
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Add two masses
You will need: Beam balance, 1 kg, ½ kg and ¼ kg masses, Two small bags of sand, Exercise book

1. Measure the mass of each bag using kilogramme masses.

2. Add the two masses in your book.

3. Put both bags in one pan and measure the total. Compare it with your addition.

4. Work out 156 kg + 89 kg in columns, then add 89 kg + 156 kg as a check.

5. Take turns recording the answer so that one person does not do all the writing.

## Practice

1. Add 64 kg and 29 kg.

2. Add 275 kg and 148 kg.

3. Add 1½ kg and ¾ kg.

4. A trader has 1,250 kg of maize and buys 875 kg more. What is the total mass?

## Answers to practice

1. 93 kg

2. 423 kg

3. 2¼ kg

4. 2,125 kg

## Summary
• Add kilogrammes in columns and carry when a column is 10 or more.
• Add halves and quarters, changing 2 halves into 1 kg.
• Check by adding in the other order, or by weighing both objects together.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Subtracting mass in kilogrammes
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: SUBTRACTING MASS IN KILOGRAMMES
=========================================

## What you will learn
• Subtract kilogrammes, regrouping when a digit is too small.
• Subtract halves and quarters of a kilogramme.

Curriculum outcomes: d) subtract mass involving kilogrammes in real- life situations

## Introduction
A store had 70 kg of beans. Customers bought 28 kg. Subtraction tells you the mass that is still in the store. You can check a small subtraction on the beam balance.

## Notes

Write the larger mass on top. Subtract the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds. If a top digit is smaller than the digit below it, regroup.

### Whole kilogrammes
Subtract 28 kg from 70 kg.

- Ones: 0 is smaller than 8. Regroup 1 ten. The tens become 6, and the ones become 10.
- 10 − 8 = 2.
- Tens: 6 − 2 = 4.
- 42 kg remain.

Subtract 175 kg from 400 kg.

- Ones: regroup, 10 − 5 = 5.
- Tens: the tens digit became 9 after regrouping from the hundreds, then 9 − 7 = 2.
- Hundreds: 3 − 1 = 2.
- 225 kg remain.

Check: 225 + 175 = 400.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Subtracting mass in kilogrammes — Key words
studyPages.body:
### Halves and quarters
5 kg − 1½ kg. First take away 1 kg, leaving 4 kg. Then take away ½ kg, leaving 3½ kg.

1 kg − ¼ kg = ¾ kg.

½ kg − ¼ kg = ¼ kg.

2¼ kg − ¾ kg: the quarters are 1 quarter minus 3 quarters, so regroup 1 whole as 4 quarters. You then have 1 whole and 5 quarters, minus 3 quarters, which is 1 whole and 2 quarters. Two quarters are a half, so the answer is 1½ kg.

On a balance, you can check 1 kg − ¼ kg by removing a ¼ kg mass from a 1 kg side and seeing that ¾ kg remains to balance it.

## Key words
• difference in mass — how much heavier one object is, or how much mass is left
• regroup — to change 1 ten into 10 ones, or 1 kg into halves or quarters, so you can subtract

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Subtract 28 kg from 70 kg.

Working:
1. Regroup 1 ten: 10 − 8 = 2.
2. Tens: 6 − 2 = 4.

Answer: 42 kg

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Subtract 175 kg from 400 kg.

Working:
1. 400 − 175.
2. Check by adding 225 + 175.

Answer: 225 kg

## Worked examples

### Example 3
Subtract 1½ kg from 5 kg.

Working:
1. 5 − 1 = 4.
2. 4 − ½ = 3½.

Answer: 3½ kg

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Subtracting mass in kilogrammes — Mass left on the pan
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Mass left on the pan
You will need: Beam balance, 1 kg and ¼ kg masses, A bag of sand, Exercise book

1. Make a bag of sand with mass 1 kg. Remove sand until the bag balances ¾ kg. Say which subtraction you did.

2. In your book, subtract 28 kg from 70 kg and check by adding.

3. Solve 2¼ kg − ¾ kg and explain the regrouping of 1 kg into quarters.

4. Write one real situation, such as selling maize or using cooking fat, where you subtract mass.

5. If you can, play a digital game about mass and record one subtraction from it.

## Practice

1. Subtract 46 kg from 90 kg.

2. A store had 500 kg of rice and sold 275 kg. How much rice is left?

3. Subtract ¾ kg from 2¼ kg.

4. How do you check that 400 − 175 = 225?

## Answers to practice

1. 44 kg

2. 225 kg

3. 1½ kg

4. Add 225 and 175. The sum should be 400.

## Summary
• Subtract kilogrammes in columns, regrouping when you need to.
• Check by adding the answer to the mass that was taken away.
• Change 1 kg into quarters when the fraction on top is too small.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Using the kilogramme in daily life — A fair measurement
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: USING THE KILOGRAMME IN DAILY LIFE
============================================

## What you will learn
• Describe work in which people measure mass in kilogrammes.
• Explain why an accurate mass is fair to both the buyer and the seller.

Curriculum outcomes: e) appreciate kilogramme as a unit of measuring mass

## Introduction
Bread, sugar, maize flour, meat and animal feed are sold by the kilogramme. A correct balance protects the customer and the seller.

## Notes

People use the kilogramme in many jobs.

- A shopkeeper weighs flour, rice, sugar and beans.
- A farmer weighs a harvest before taking it to market.
- A cook measures ingredients so that a recipe turns out as planned.
- A health worker may record a person's mass as one fact about growth. That reading is done on a proper scale, not guessed.
- A builder orders sand or cement by the kilogramme or by a known bag size.

### A fair measurement
If a beam is not level and the seller still calls the mass 2 kg, the customer may receive less than 2 kg. If the masses themselves are wrong, both sides are cheated. Using a true 1 kg, ½ kg or ¼ kg mass, and waiting until the beam is level, is an honest measurement.

An electronic balance must start at zero. A container left on the balance adds its own mass. Put the container on first, set the reading back to zero, then add the food. The screen then shows the mass of the food only.

### Sharing the tools
In class, one balance serves many learners. Each person needs a turn to measure, and the masses must be put back so the next group can work. That is a fair use of a shared tool.

The kilogramme is worth learning because it is the same unit in a market, a shop and a store. Once you can add and subtract kilogrammes, you can find a total order or the mass that remains after a sale.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Using the kilogramme in daily life — A fair market stall
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• accurate — measured carefully so that the result matches the true mass
• zero — the reading on an electronic balance before the object is placed, or after a container is set aside

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A customer buys 2 kg of beans and 1½ kg of rice. What is the total mass?

Working:
1. 2 + 1½ = 3½.
2. The shopkeeper should pack 3½ kg altogether.

Answer: 3½ kg

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A sack of 50 kg has 12 kg sold from it. What mass remains?

Working:
1. 50 − 12 = 38.

Answer: 38 kg

## Activity: A fair market stall
You will need: Beam balance, 1 kg and ½ kg masses, Bags of sand to stand for food, Price cards are not needed

1. Role-play a seller and a buyer. The buyer asks for 1½ kg of 'beans' made from sand.

2. The seller measures 1 kg and ½ kg while the buyer watches the beam.

3. The buyer checks that the beam is level before accepting the bag.

4. Swap roles. Then subtract: if 2 kg was on the table and 1½ kg was sold, what mass is left?

5. Talk about why both people should be able to see the balance.

studyPages.title: Revision quiz
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. A cook uses 1½ kg of flour and ½ kg of sugar. What is the total mass of the two ingredients?

2. A farmer harvested 86 kg of beans and kept 29 kg for the family. What mass can be taken to market?

3. Why should an electronic balance read zero before you put food on it?

4. Name two workers who measure mass in kilogrammes.

## Answers to practice

1. 2 kg

2. 57 kg

3. So that the screen shows the mass of the food, and not an old reading or the mass of an empty container.

4. Any two, such as a shopkeeper, a farmer, a cook or a health worker.

## Summary
• The kilogramme is used for food, farm produce and many goods.
• A level beam, true masses and a zeroed electronic balance give a fair measure.
• Add to find a total order and subtract to find what remains.

REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. When is the mass of an object equal to the masses in the other pan of a beam balance?
   A. When the object pan is down
   B. When the beam is level
   C. When the mass pan is down

2. Five masses of 1 kg balance a bag. What is the mass of the bag?

3. How many half kilogrammes make 3 kg?
   A. 3
   B. 5
   C. 6
   D. 8

4. An object balances three masses of ½ kg. What is its mass?

5. How many quarter kilogrammes make 2 kg?

6. Add 48 kg and 37 kg.
   A. 75 kg
   B. 85 kg
   C. 85 g
   D. 11 kg

7. Add 2½ kg and 1¾ kg.

8. Subtract 28 kg from 70 kg.

9. Subtract 175 kg from 400 kg.
   A. 225 kg
   B. 235 kg
   C. 375 kg
   D. 575 kg

10. Why should a seller wait until the beam is level before saying the mass is 2 kg?

studyPages.title: Quiz answers
studyPages.body:
ANSWERS
=======

1. B. When the beam is level
   A level beam means the two sides have the same mass.

2. 5 kg
   5 × 1 kg = 5 kg.

3. C. 6
   Each kilogramme has 2 halves, so 3 × 2 = 6.

4. 1½ kg
   3 × ½ = 1½ kg.

5. 8
   Each kilogramme has 4 quarters, so 2 × 4 = 8.

6. B. 85 kg
   8 + 7 = 15, write 5 carry 1; 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. The total is 85 kg.

7. 4¼ kg
   ½ + ¾ = 1¼, and 2 + 1 + 1¼ = 4¼ kg.

8. 42 kg
   70 − 28 = 42.

9. A. 225 kg
   400 − 175 = 225. Check: 225 + 175 = 400.

10. Only a level beam shows that the goods really have a mass of 2 kg.
   If the beam is not level, the customer may get more or less than 2 kg.
